choices: Someone always pays for media, so free news calls for media literacy
All media are propaganda and should be avoided
Only state-owned media are biased, while privately owned media stay neutral
Journalists should work for free to stay independent
why: Journalists need salaries, so media are funded by governments, corporations or advertisers. Since we consume it for free, we need critical thinking to judge whether it is accurate or biased.

q: The opening slide of the mass media lecture is titled 'media dependence'. Which point from the lecture does it connect to?
choices: We rely on mostly free media, so we must judge its accuracy
Media depend on the government for permission to publish anything
Journalists depend on bloggers for most of their stories
Advertisers depend on viewers to vote for their products
why: We get much of our picture of the world from media we don't pay for, and the forces behind those media shape what we receive. That dependence is why media literacy matters.

q: Mass media are...
choices: Communication built to reach and influence very large audiences
Small outlets that target a specific, specialised niche audience
Private messages exchanged between individuals on messaging apps
Only television, radio and newspapers
why: Small outlets aimed at a specific audience are niche media. Today mass media also include the internet and social media.

q: A Tashkent food blogger who started filming for friends now has 1.5 million followers and posts daily news about city life. According to the lecture, this blogger has...
choices: Become mass media in their own right
Remained niche media, since they're not a TV channel
Become exempt from questions of bias
Become part of the sourcing filter
why: The lecture says that today ordinary people can become bloggers and turn into mass media themselves, reaching and influencing very large audiences.

q: Which example does the lecture use to show that the media can live up to their role as credible watchdogs?
choices: Reporters exposing Rockefeller's oil monopoly
Herman and Chomsky's study of the five filters
BBC coverage of AI research funded by tech billionaires
The rise of short news videos on Instagram
why: Investigative reporting uncovered how Rockefeller built his monopoly through cartels with supply-chain companies, and the government then split the corporation up. Media can expose bad actors.

q: What does the lecture mean by 'sensationalism and the news as entertainment'?
choices: Audiences want a quick 'dopamine hit' and avoid in-depth analysis
Advertisers pay for the audience's attention rather than for the content
Outlets slant stories toward their followers' views
Journalists expose wrongdoing by powerful people
why: Celebrity news, shock videos and Shorts or Reels feed the demand for entertainment. Slanting stories toward followers is bias in the news.

q: A news channel's top story is 'SHOCKING: celebrity's wedding guest list leaked!' while a new tax law gets a 20-second mention at the end. Which issue with news coverage does this show?
choices: Sensationalism
Bias in the news
The sourcing filter
Credible investigative coverage
why: Celebrity shock content goes first because it delivers a dopamine hit, while the story that needs analysis gets almost none.

q: According to the lecture, why do some media outlets become biased?
choices: To align with the needs and interests of their followers
Because journalists cannot read scientific papers
Because the law requires them to take sides
Because sensational stories are always the true ones
why: To keep their audience, outlets may skew stories toward what their followers want to hear.

q: Two outlets cover the same fuel-price rise. One, popular with government supporters, headlines 'Prices adjusted to world markets'; the other, popular with critics, runs 'Families hit by price shock.' Which issue does this show?
choices: Bias in the news
Depth of news analysis
Credibility of news coverage
Media dependence
why: Each outlet tailors the same facts to its own followers' views.

q: What does the lecture say about the depth of news analysis today?
choices: Competing for attention pushes even big outlets to shallow short-form content
The internet has made news analysis far deeper and longer than ever before
Only state-owned media have moved to short-form content
Short videos are now more accurate than long articles
why: Registered outlets compete with bloggers and foreign media for our time, so even big names follow the short-form trend to keep their followers.

q: A respected national newspaper replaces its long investigations with 40-second vertical videos because they get more views. What does this illustrate?
choices: Shallow depth of news analysis
The flak filter
Credibility of news coverage
Media literacy
why: Competing for attention, the outlet trades depth for short content that is easier to consume.

q: Why does the lecture call science reporting a 'slippery slope'?
choices: 'Research shows...' makes people stop thinking critically
Scientific findings change too quickly to report accurately
Scientists refuse to speak to journalists
Science news is always sensational
why: Because a claim sounds scientific, people start believing it without analysis. Hence the checklist of questions for science reporting.

q: Which of these is on the lecture's checklist for evaluating scientific reporting?
choices: What is the background of the reporter?
How many views did the report get?
Does the report confirm what I already believe?
Is the reporter popular on social media?
why: The six questions: who is making the claim, the source's credentials and funding, the reporter's background, where the study was first published, how other authorities respond, and whether the report is biased.

q: A glowing study says AI tools will double workers' productivity. You find it was funded by companies run by Sam Altman and Elon Musk. Which checklist question has flagged a concern?
choices: What are the credentials and funding of the source?
How might different groups of people interpret the message?
What techniques are used to hold attention?
Where was the study first published?
why: Results can be skewed toward what funders want. This is the professor's own example: upbeat AI research backed by Altman, Amodei or Musk.

q: Kun.uz reports 'Scientists find green tea prevents memory loss.' What does the lecture tell you to do?
choices: Find the original paper and check its journal is credible
Trust it, since a big news site wouldn't get science wrong
Check what readers say in the comments
Dismiss it, since science news is always fake
why: Outlets like Kun.uz, BBC or CNN report on research rather than doing it, so ask where it was first published and whether that journal is credible.

q: One researcher claims a new diet cures diabetes. The news story quotes no other scientists, and medical associations haven't commented. Which checklist question exposes the weakness?
choices: How are other authorities in the field responding?
What is the purpose of the message?
What was your reaction to the message?
What techniques are used to attract and hold your attention?
why: Check whether a finding is one-sided or broadly agreed. A single unconfirmed voice is weak support.

q: A paper found a 'small, possibly coincidental' link between screen time and poor sleep. A youth news channel headlines it: 'Phones DESTROY your sleep, science proves.' Which checklist question applies most directly?
choices: Is the report biased?
What is the background of the reporter?
What are the credentials and funding of the source?
How might different people interpret the message?
why: The outlet has exaggerated the original finding to suit its audience, which is exactly what the 'is the report biased?' question checks.

q: According to the lecture, media literacy is...
choices: The ability to understand and critically analyse the influence of mass media
Knowing how to use media apps and platforms
The ability to create popular content that spreads quickly on social media
Following the news every day
why: The professor stresses that it isn't just knowing how to use media. The same applies to social-media and AI literacy.

q: Aziza writes excellent ChatGPT prompts but has never asked who builds it, who profits from it, or how it might mislead her. By the lecture's standard, what does she lack?
choices: AI literacy in the full sense: critically analysing its influence
Nothing, since knowing how to use a tool well is what literacy means
Knowledge of the sourcing filter
Skill at producing short-form content
why: Literacy, whether media, social-media or AI, means understanding and critically analysing a thing's influence, not just using it.

q: Which of these is one of the media-analysis questions from the lecture?
choices: What techniques are used to attract and hold your attention?
How many likes did the message get?
Is the message from a country I trust?
Does the message agree with my friends' views?
why: The eleven questions cover who made it, its purpose, techniques, values, your reaction and why, your interpretation, others' interpretations, bias, reasoning and facts, and effects.

q: Under 'what techniques are used to attract and hold your attention?', what does the lecture tell you to look for?
choices: Scare tactics and doom-and-gloom scenarios
Who funded the original study
Whether other experts agree
The reporter's background
why: Fear and gloom are classic attention grabbers. The other options belong to the science-reporting checklist.

q: Before trusting a viral article praising a new shopping mall, Dildora checks who published it and finds it's the developer's own PR site. Which media-analysis questions is she using?
choices: Who created the message, and what is its purpose?
How might different people interpret the same message?
What was your reaction, and why?
What are its possible effects on society?
why: The 'who created it' and 'what is its purpose' questions ask who is behind a message and what it is trying to achieve. A developer's PR site exists to promote the mall.

q: Analysing a news story about a new law, Bobur asks whether it reflects a particular political or moral viewpoint. Which analysis question is he using?
choices: What values and points of view are represented?
What was your reaction to the message?
What are the possible effects on individuals and society?
Who created the message?
why: That question looks for the political and moral views a message carries.

q: A headline makes Nigora furious before she has even read the article. Which pair of analysis questions asks her to examine this?
choices: What was your reaction, and why did it make you feel that way?
Who created the message, and what is its purpose?
Is it biased, and is it backed by facts?
How might others read it, and what effects might it have on society?
why: These two questions turn the analysis on your own response, which a headline may have steered before you saw the facts.

q: A crime report says 'young men from the regions are behind most street thefts', based on a single incident. Which analysis question applies most directly?
choices: Is the message biased?
What was your reaction to the message?
Who created the message?
Is your interpretation reasonable and well informed?
why: The lecture's bias check looks for hasty generalisations and stories skewed for or against particular groups.

q: A viral post says 'Bread prices will triple next month' but cites no data, no officials and no sources. Which analysis question exposes this most directly?
choices: Is the message backed by good reasoning and facts?
What was your reaction to the message?
How might different people interpret it?
What values and points of view are represented in the message?
why: That question tells you to check the premises, the evidence and where the sources come from.

q: A report on a new metro line reads as great news to a commuter and as bad news to a shop owner whose shop will be demolished for it. Which analysis question captures this?
choices: How might different people interpret the message?
Who created the message?
Is the message biased toward or against certain groups?
What is the purpose of the message?
why: We each read messages through our own worldview, history and interests, so the same report can mean very different things to different people.

q: What does the last of the media-analysis questions ask?
choices: What are its possible effects on individuals and society?
How much did the message cost to produce?
Which platform gave the message the most views, likes and shares?
Who funded the original research?
why: It asks how the message may affect people individually, locally and across society. Funding of research belongs to the science-reporting checklist.

q: In the lecture, being in an echo chamber means...
choices: Following only sources that share one worldview, so you see one side
A story is repeated across many outlets until people accept it as true
Advertisers buy the audience's attention
A reporter loses access to official sources
why: The professor's examples: following only Uzbek bloggers, only Russian-language channels, or only Western corporate media like BBC, CNN and the New York Times.

q: Otabek gets all his news from Russian-language Telegram channels with one political line, and his friend follows only BBC, CNN and the New York Times. What does the professor advise both of them?
choices: Seek alternative media to see the other side of the coin
Stick with one trusted source to avoid confusion
Stop following the news altogether
Follow only officially registered outlets
why: Both are in echo chambers. He suggests alternative media, including unregistered bloggers and international coverage of Uzbekistan, for different perspectives.
